planting.note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions, or set container-grown plants out in spring once nights stay above 55F, placing them in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this slow grower resents cold drafts, soggy roots, and sudden moves between light levels, so acclimate it gradually.

directions: Propagate from semi-hardwood stem cuttings rooted under warmth and humidity, then grow in well-drained, fertile soil in bright, filtered shade protected from direct midday sun. The nearly round, coin-shaped leaflets are borne in clusters along stiff, jointed, bamboo-like stems and often show irregular cream-gray marbling or a pale marginal band, giving the shrub a sculptural, almost bonsai-like presence even on young plants. Growth is slow and upright, making it a long-lived specimen for a shaded courtyard bed or a large container that can be moved indoors where winters are cold. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since both drought stress and wet feet quickly cause leaf drop.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Root woody stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions, or plant established nursery specimens in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade with protection from wind, which can shred the thin leaflets; this tender shrub is grown outdoors only in zones 10-11 and otherwise kept as a container plant brought in before cold weather.

directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings and grow on in fertile, well-drained soil in filtered light, since the deeply lobed, toothed leaflets can scorch in strong direct sun. Leaf shape and variegation are highly variable even within a single plant, ranging from broad and geranium-like to narrow and lacy, with many selections showing an irregular creamy-white margin. Left unpruned it becomes an open, multi-stemmed small tree, but it also takes readily to shearing and has long been used as a dense informal hedge or screen in frost-free gardens. Shelter from strong wind and cold drafts, both of which cause rapid leaf loss on this thin-leaved aralia.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Root stem cuttings under intermittent mist or high humidity, then plant out in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade once temperatures stay reliably above 55F; keep away from cold drafts and dry indoor heating, both of which cause the finely cut foliage to drop.

directions: Propagate from stem cuttings and establish in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shaded or filtered-light positions sheltered from wind. The pinnately compound leaves are finely divided into narrow, toothed, almost fern-like or parsley-like segments, some selections further crested or twisted, giving the plant a delicate, airy texture distinct from the coarser-leaved aralia species. It grows as an upright, lightly branched shrub and is often kept pruned and container-grown as a houseplant or patio specimen outside its frost-free growing range. Protect from cold, dry air and direct hot sun, both of which quickly damage the thin leaflets.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions, then grow on in rich, well-drained soil in bright, filtered light; place outdoors only after nights stay above 55F and bring containers indoors well before the first fall frost, since this cultivar is tender below zone 10.

directions: Grow from rooted stem cuttings in well-drained, fertile soil in bright indirect light or light shade, since deep shade dulls the foliage color while harsh direct sun can scorch it. Unlike the plain green species, 'Fabian' produces thick, nearly circular leaflets in a deep bronze-black to purplish tone with a glossy, almost lacquered sheen, held on compact, upright stems that stay dense without much pruning. It is widely grown as a houseplant and dish-garden or bonsai subject for its unusual near-black coloration, and also works as a low accent shrub in frost-free shaded landscapes. Avoid overwatering and cold, drafty locations, which both lead to rapid leaf drop on this slow-growing cultivar.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
